intent.claim: Scalable tactics assume a force already in motion; at the start none exists, so disproportionate personal effort is the only lever available.
intent.mechanism: Two levers acting on the same load: the 'scalable' lever (word-of-mouth, brand trust) requires pre-existing momentum to transmit any force, so at zero momentum it moves nothing; the 'unscalable' lever (direct personal effort) supplies force from the founder directly and works precisely because the user count is tiny.
intent.changes: At zero-momentum the scalable lever is slack and transmits no force; the unscalable lever is taut and moves the load — the difference is whether the lever needs a crowd that doesn't exist yet.
intent.resting: Left: a scalable lever connected to an absent flywheel, hanging useless. Right: an unscalable lever driven straight by the founder's hand, actually turning the load.

claim_at_rest.read_claim: When you have very few users, growth tactics that scale do nothing because there's no crowd to drive them, so the founder's own unscalable effort is the only thing that moves growth.
read_evidence: Title: "Scalable levers need a crowd. At the start, you are the only force."

The reader's "crowd to drive them" matches "force already in motion," and "unscalable effort is the only thing" matches "disproportionate personal effort is the only lever." On the right, a present founder connects to the load by a taut line, the wheel shows motion dots, and the bar is nearly full. "Scalable levers need a crowd" and "word of mouth, a trusted brand" are the slide's own framing, not Graham's argument. His stated reasons for doing unscalable things are founder shyness and laziness, underestimating compound growth, and the fact that a startup has nothing to lose. intent.title: Recruit Users One by One
intent.claim: Users are won one at a time by hand, and those small numbers compound into enormous ones through sustained weekly growth.
intent.mechanism: Input: founder personally reaches and sets up one individual user (not broadcast-and-wait). Relation: each added user compounds at a weekly growth rate. Output: a tiny starting base multiplies over time — the manual act is small, the compounding is not.
intent.resting: A staged progression: one founder handing setup to one user (Collison installation), then the compounding count ticking up week by week along the same ignition arc.

claim_at_rest.read_claim: Winning early users one at a time by hand, like Stripe's on-the-spot setups, looks small, but growing 10% a week compounds from 100 users to about 2 million in two years.

Left body text: "One person, one setup, right now... it is what supplies the 10% you need each week"
Chart labels: "100 · start", "≈14,000 · 1 yr", "≈2,000,000 · 2 yrs"; slider label "+10% / WEEK"
Readouts: "WEEK 104", "TOTAL USERS 2,017,619", "WIN BY HAND THIS WEEK +201,762"
evidence: Title: "Recruit users one by one — the act is small, the compounding isn't"

claim_at_rest.reasoning: The reader's claim includes both parts of the intended claim: users are won one at a time by hand, and those small numbers grow into huge ones through steady weekly growth (10%/week, 100 to about 2M). The causal link, that hand-recruiting supplies the weekly growth that compounds, is there. The concrete figures and the Stripe example are supporting detail and don't change the claim.

evidence: Left figure: "FOUNDER" icon → dashed arrow → "SETUP" box → dashed arrow → "ONE USER" icon, captioned "ON THE SPOT · IN THE ROOM"
Right chart: an exponential curve from "100 · start" at WK 0 through "≈14,000 · 1 yr" at WK 52 to "≈2,000,000 · 2 yrs" at WK 104
Readouts: "WEEK 104", "TOTAL USERS 2,017,619", "WIN BY HAND THIS WEEK +201,762"

mechanism_shown.reasoning: The compounding part is clearly drawn. The curve has axes, and you can trace it from a tiny start to a huge end, with week-by-week controls and a growth-rate label on the slider. The manual input is also drawn, as a founder → setup → one-user flow. But nothing visual connects that single hand-won user to the 10% weekly growth on the chart. Only the sentence "it is what supplies the 10% you need each week" makes that link, and the two panels sit side by side without any connection drawn between them. Since one link exists only in text, this scores a 3.

distortions: "WIN BY HAND THIS WEEK +201,762" at week 104, combined with "it is what supplies the 10% you need each week": the slide says manual, one-at-a-time recruiting keeps delivering 10% weekly growth all the way to 2M users. The source says manual recruiting only gets growth started. Founders then do different things at scale and gradually switch to less manual methods, and growth eventually slows. The slide leaves out that condition.

Minor: the slide gives +201,762 as this week's gain, but that is 10% of the current total, which is next week's target. The actual gain from week 103 to 104 would be about 183k. This is an internal inconsistency in the simulation, not a claim taken from the source.
evidence: The headline "Recruit users one by one — the act is small, the compounding isn't" matches the source's point that founders "underestimate the power of compound growth".

The panel "STRIPE'S 'COLLISON INSTALLATION'" quotes "We'll send you a link." (struck through) and "Right then, give me your laptop." Both are exact quotes from the source. The first is what "more diffident founders" say; the second is what the Collison brothers said.

The chart labels "100 · start", "≈14,000 · 1 yr", "≈2,000,000 · 2 yrs" and "+10% / WEEK" match the source: "If you have 100 users... grow 10% a week... After a year you'll have 14,000 users, and after 2 years you'll have 2 million."

"WIN BY HAND THIS WEEK +201,762" at week 104, together with the caption "One person, one setup, right now. That is the whole manual act — and it is what supplies the 10% you need each week."

The source says the opposite: "You'll be doing different things when you're acquiring users a thousand at a time, and growth has to slow down eventually... start by recruiting users manually and then gradually switch to less manual methods."
fidelity.reasoning: Every quote, name and anchor number on the slide (Stripe, the Collison installation, 100 users, 10% a week, about 14,000 after 1 year, about 2M after 2 years) traces to the source, and nothing is invented. However, the interactive counter and caption frame the entire 2M curve as users "won by hand", which drops the source's explicit caveat that manual recruiting is only the starting crank, later replaced by less manual methods. That is a material distortion of the source's main point, so the score is capped at 2.

intent.title: Delight Beyond What's Reasonable
intent.claim: With only a handful of users you can give each an insanely great experience, and that attentiveness compensates for a buggy, incomplete product.
intent.mechanism: Input: founder attentiveness per user (feasible only at small scale). Relation: total experience quality = product quality + attentiveness; attentiveness fills the gap the incomplete product leaves. Output: users feel delighted even when the product is rough.
intent.operate: The reader raises an 'attentiveness' dial while the product stays buggy/incomplete.
intent.changes: As attentiveness rises, the overall experience meter climbs into 'insanely great' even though the product bar stays low — and the dial is only reachable while user count is small.
intent.aha: You can deliver an insanely great experience on a bad product — the missing product quality is made up by attention no big company could afford.
intent.resting: A low, gap-filled product bar beside an experience meter sitting low, with the attentiveness dial at its resting minimum — the gap plainly visible and unfilled.

claim_at_rest.read_claim: When you have only a few users, the founder's personal attention can make being your user an insanely great experience even when the product itself is rough, because experience = product + attentiveness.
read_evidence: Delight beyond what's reasonable
What should be insanely great isn't the product — it's the experience of being your user.
EXPERIENCE = PRODUCT + ATTENTIVENESS
Like a new restaurant where the owner personally greets every table — the food may be uneven, but the care makes people fall in love and come back.
Wufoo sent every new user a hand-written thank-you note. Tim Cook can't send you a note. You can.
Instrument: PRODUCT bar labeled 'BUGS · GAPS', EXPERIENCE bar at 'ROUGH' with markers 'FINE' and 'INSANELY GREAT'
USERS YOU HAVE 5 / 50 / 5,000; FOUNDER ATTENTIVENESS 0–4; 'Product stays at 30 — attention fills the gap.'

"Product stays at 30 — attention fills the gap."
PRODUCT bar labeled 'BUGS · GAPS'
"the food may be uneven, but the care makes people fall in love"
claim_at_rest.reasoning: The reader's claim has every part of the intended one. It names the condition (only a few users), the mechanism (personal attention from the founder), the result (an insanely great experience) and the compensation (it makes up for a rough product with bugs and gaps). The phrase 'attention fills the gap' carries the compensatory relationship directly. Nothing important is missing or added.

evidence: Two side-by-side bars labelled "PRODUCT" and "EXPERIENCE". The Product bar is mostly hatched, with "BUGS · GAPS" in the empty upper part and a grey fill up to the "ROUGH" level. The Experience bar has threshold lines labelled "— INSANELY GREAT", "— FINE" and "— ROUGH".

Controls: "USERS YOU HAVE" (5 / 50 / 5,000) and "FOUNDER ATTENTIVENESS" (0–4). At 5,000 users, levels 1–4 are struck through and the caption reads "Out of reach at this scale." At 50 users, only 3 and 4 are struck through, and the caption reads "thin — some notes".
Attentiveness stays at "0" in every screenshot. The Experience bar never rises above "ROUGH". The only change is a thin cyan sliver on top of the bar at 5,000 users.
The additive relation appears only as text: "EXPERIENCE = PRODUCT + ATTENTIVENESS" and "Product stays at 30 — attention fills the gap."
mechanism_shown.reasoning: The figure does have real structure. The product bar with its gaps sits next to an experience bar marked with quality levels, and the controls visibly show that more users means less attentiveness is available, since buttons get disabled. That makes the scale → attentiveness link readable from the figure. But no screenshot shows attentiveness actually filling the experience bar toward "INSANELY GREAT". The core link, product + attentiveness = delight, is only stated in the equation and the caption. So one key link rests on text, not on the drawing.

evidence: At rest, with users at "5" and attentiveness at "0", the EXPERIENCE bar is grey up to "— ROUGH". It matches the PRODUCT bar, which is labelled "BUGS · GAPS".

Clicking attentiveness "1" adds a cyan segment above the grey. Clicking "2" brings it up to "— FINE". Clicking "4" brings it past "— INSANELY GREAT". The PRODUCT bar does not change, and the caption says "Product stays at 30 — attention fills the gap."

Clicking users "5,000" resets attentiveness to 0. Buttons 1–4 become struck-through and disabled, with the captions "Out of reach at this scale." and "≈ attention per user: none — you are Tim Cook now".

device_works.reasoning: The planned operation works immediately and is easy to read. Raising attentiveness stacks cyan on a fixed grey product base until the bar passes 'insanely great'. The user-count control limits which attentiveness levels you can pick, and the steps in between (50 users allows only up to 2) show the trade-off well. The equation 'EXPERIENCE = PRODUCT + ATTENTIVENESS' matches the stacked bars, so a first-time viewer can reach the aha. The control is a row of discrete buttons, not a dial, and there is a leftover cyan sliver at 5,000 users, but both issues are minor.

distortions: At 5,000 users the slide says "attention per user: none — you are Tim Cook now" and "Out of reach at this scale." The source pushes back on the worry that delight won't scale. It says having too many users to delight 'would be a great problem to have' and 'delighting customers scales better than you expected.' It also says Wufoo kept up its notes 'surprisingly long.' The toy model shows a hard cutoff that the source argues against, though it is a secondary, illustrative part of the slide.
evidence: Body text: "What should be insanely great isn't the product — it's the experience of being your user" matches the source: "It's not the product that should be insanely great, but the experience of being your user."

The analogy and the sample note are marked as illustrative, and the numbers are obviously toy values. There are two flaws. The slide drops Wufoo's 'for as long as they could' qualifier, which is minor. The interactive scaling behavior, where attention drops to none and delight is 'out of reach' at 5,000 users, leans against the source's point that delight scales better than expected. This is a mild distortion inside a toy control, not a core claim, so the score is 3 rather than 4.

intent.claim: Doing things by hand is also the tightest feedback loop — the effort that grows the company and the effort that improves the product are the same effort.
intent.mechanism: Input: founder over-engages directly with early users. Relation: that single act splits into two returns — it drives growth AND surfaces exactly what's broken/confusing/wanted. Output: product improves from direct contact; automating this stage would sever the feedback and blind you.
intent.resting: One stream of founder effort forking into two outputs — a growth line and a product-improvement line — with a feedback arrow running from users back into the product; a crossed-out 'automate' shows the loop severed.

intent.title: Start Narrow to Catch Fire
intent.claim: Concentrating limited effort on a deliberately tiny market builds the density needed to catch, where the same effort spread thin dies out.
intent.mechanism: Input: a fixed amount of founder effort (heat). Relation: concentrated on a small market it exceeds the ignition threshold and self-sustains; spread across a large market it falls below threshold everywhere and dissipates. Output: saturation of a small space, then it can jump.
intent.operate: The reader adjusts how wide the market/field the same flame is spread across.
intent.changes: Spread wide, the flame thins below threshold and dies; packed onto concentrated kindling it crosses the threshold, catches, and then jumps outward.
intent.aha: The same flame that dies across a whole field catches when packed tight — critical mass is about density, not total size.
intent.resting: A concentrated pile of kindling just beginning to glow at the ignition threshold, a wide unlit field waiting beside it.

intent.claim: A startup is a vector — what you'll build plus the unscalable effort to start it — and that early push often becomes the company's permanent DNA.
intent.mechanism: Composition of two components into one vector: 'what you build' (direction) added to 'the unscalable things you do' (magnitude of effort). Relation: the effort component isn't discarded scaffolding — it persists as habits (obsessing over users, learning by contact) baked into the company for good.
intent.resting: Two arrows composed tip-to-tail into a single resultant vector — 'build' plus 'unscalable effort' — with the effort component annotated as carrying forward into the company's lasting DNA rather than being thrown away.

items.q: What does the car-engine crank metaphor say about how startups take off?
items.ref: Startups don't usually take off on their own. The founders have to push them through a separate, laborious start-up phase, like hand-cranking an engine, and after that the engine keeps running by itself.
items.answer: A startup is like a hand-cranked early car: the engine won't run until the founders turn the crank by hand. Once it passes a catch point, it keeps running on its own as self-sustaining growth, but if they let go before that point it stalls.
items.why: Gets the key idea: founders have to hand-crank the startup through a hard start-up phase, and after that it runs on its own.

items.q: Why does the essay argue that recruiting users one by one is worth it even though the numbers seem tiny at first?
items.ref: Because of compound growth. If you keep up a steady weekly growth rate like 10%, small absolute gains build into huge numbers (about 14,000 users after one year and 2 million after two), so manual recruiting can get you to scale.
items.answer: Each user is won by hand, and this small manual act (like Stripe's 'Collison installation') supplies the 10% weekly growth you need. That growth compounds: 100 users becomes about 14,000 after 1 year and about 2,000,000 after 2 years.
items.why: Explains that steady 10% weekly growth compounds, and gives the 14,000 and 2 million figures.

items.q: What mistake do inexperienced founders and investors make when they judge early startups, and what question should they ask instead?
items.ref: They judge fragile, larval startups by the standards of established companies and dismiss them. Instead they should ask how big the company could get if the founders did the right things.
items.answer: The deck says founders wrongly treat the start as a shrunk-down version of the finished company and judge it by size, when they should judge it by motion (whether it's gaining momentum). It doesn't discuss investors or give a specific question to ask.
items.why: Catches that people judge the larval startup as if it were a small version of an established company, but leaves out investors and the 'how big could it get' question.

items.q: How can a small startup give better customer service than a big company, and why do founders often fail to see this?
items.ref: Being small lets founders give personal attention that big companies can't, like hand-written thank-you notes. Founders miss this because their standards for service were set by the big companies they've been customers of, and because engineers aren't trained in customer service.
items.answer: With only a handful of users, founders can give each one extraordinary attention, like Wufoo's hand-written thank-you notes, which a big-company CEO like Tim Cook can't send. The deck doesn't explain why founders fail to see this; it only suggests they mistakenly act as if the company were already running at full scale.
items.why: Explains how being small allows personal attention like hand-written notes, but misses why founders don't see it: their standards come from big companies, and engineers aren't trained in customer service.

items.q: In a startup's early months, how does the meaning of 'insanely great' shift, and why does over-engaging with users improve the product?
items.ref: What should be insanely great is the experience of being a user, not the product, so attentiveness can make up for a buggy, incomplete product. Engaging directly with early users also gives the best feedback, which drives the iteration that makes the product good.
items.answer: Early on, what should be 'insanely great' is not the product but the experience of being your user, where experience = product + attentiveness, so founder attention fills the gaps in a rough product. Working closely with early users also improves the product, because they show you what's broken, what confuses them and what they want, giving you the tightest feedback loop you'll ever get.
items.why: Says the user's experience, not the product, should be insanely great, and that close contact with early users gives the feedback that improves the product.

items.q: Why might a startup deliberately start in a narrow market, as Facebook did with Harvard?
items.ref: Like keeping a fire contained so it gets hot, a narrow market lets you reach critical mass quickly because the users feel the product is really for them. You can then expand from there.
items.answer: Manual effort only reaches so many people, so concentrating it on a tiny market lets you saturate and dominate it, building the density needed to catch and then spread to the next market. Spread over a wider field, the same effort is too thin to catch. Facebook launched Harvard-only, and a critical mass signed up because it felt made for them.
items.why: Covers reaching critical mass in a narrow market, users feeling the product is made for them, and spreading from there.

items.q: What benefits come from doing things manually that you plan to automate later, or from building hardware yourself, as Meraki and Pebble did?
items.ref: It lets you launch faster and avoid obstacles like large minimum factory orders. You also learn exactly what to build or automate, and in hardware you can tweak the design faster, because you've done the work yourself.
items.answer: Doing things by hand before automating them gives two returns: users arrive, and direct contact shows you exactly what to fix, so the product improves. Building hardware yourself, and Meraki and Pebble, are not covered.
items.why: Mentions learning what to fix by doing things by hand, but misses launching faster, avoiding minimum factory orders, and the hardware points.

items.q: Why does the essay reject the 'Big Launch' and big-company partnerships, and what does it mean to think of startup ideas as vectors rather than scalars?
items.ref: Startups are like powered aircraft, not projectiles: success depends on sustained effort and on how happy you make your first users, not on initial velocity, and strategies that skip the effort are suspect. A startup idea should be seen as a pair: what you'll build plus the unscalable things you'll do to get started, and ideally those things become a permanent part of the company's DNA.
items.answer: The Big Launch and big-company partnerships are not covered. On vectors, the deck says a startup is what you'll build (the direction) plus the unscalable things you do to get it started (the magnitude of effort), and those early habits, such as obsessing over users, often become the company's permanent DNA.
items.why: Gets the idea as a pair of what you build plus the unscalable things, becoming company DNA, but says the Big Launch and partnerships aren't covered and leaves out the powered-aircraft point.
